title: San Miguel County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: San Miguel County wells run about 182 ft deep with 7 gpm median yield. See local drilling costs, water levels, and risks before you buy or build.
h1: Water wells in San Miguel County, Colorado
intro_html:
San Miguel County wells are classic mountain hard-rock wells: a lot of fractured bedrock, depths all over the map, and some very strong producers right next to tight spots. With 3,379 permits on record and 2,016 wells reporting depth, there’s enough data to see what you’re likely to hit before you buy land or bid a new well.

I’ll walk through how deep wells usually go here, how much water they tend to make, what the drilling cost numbers look like, and what risks I’d check on any parcel in this county.

sections.heading: How deep wells go in San Miguel County
sections.html:
Across San Miguel County, reported well depths center around a 182 ft median. The middle half of wells run from 75 to 325 ft, so most drillers will price jobs expecting something in that range, with clauses if they have to keep going.

About 31% of wells are under 100 ft, and another 38% fall between 100 and 300 ft. Another 25% run 300–600 ft, and 7% go deeper than 600 ft. The deepest well on record is 4,080 ft, which shows how unpredictable fractured mountain bedrock can be in places. Most permits list unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with a smaller share into the Dakota and Dakota Sandstone, so you’re usually chasing fractures, not a flat water table.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water to expect
sections.html:
Of the 717 wells that report a pump test, the median yield is 7.0 gpm, with the middle half between 4.0 and 12.0 gpm. That’s plenty for a typical exempt household well and some outdoor use, if your water rights allow it.

Production is mixed. About 4% of wells report under 1 gpm, which is marginal and usually needs storage or careful management. Another 21% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, workable but not generous. The bulk, 54%, produce 5–15 gpm, and 20% are over 15 gpm. In short, most wells here are solid domestic producers, but there is a real minority of low-yield holes you need to plan around.

sections.heading: Water levels and trends in the county
sections.html:
Only 201 wells report static water level, but they give a sense of what you’ll see. The overall median depth to water is 80 ft, with the middle half between 27 and 183 ft below ground. That means many pumps can sit fairly shallow even on deeper holes, which helps with long-term pump costs.

Looking by decade, median water levels were about 125 ft in the 1990s, 185 ft in the 2000s, then shallowed to 60 ft in the 2010s and 84 ft in the 2020s. That doesn’t read like a simple long-term decline; it’s more likely geology and where the wells were drilled each decade. Still, checking recent nearby measurements around places like Telluride, Norwood, Ophir or Mountain Village before buying is smart.

sections.heading: Who’s been drilling and when
sections.html:
San Miguel County’s well history picked up fast starting in the 1970s. The records show 3 permits in the 1950s and 10 in the 1960s, then a jump to 181 in the 1970s and 371 in the 1980s. Things really took off in the 1990s with 944 permits, then 849 in the 2000s, 308 in the 2010s, and 224 already in the 2020s, with new permits through 2025.

Most work is in fractured bedrock. The most active drillers on record here are Bill Kissner Drilling Inc, Valley Drilling Co., and Mccracken Well Drilling Inc. A majority of permits are domestic or household use at 63%, with 11% stock, 5% irrigation, and about 22% monitoring wells, which fits the mix of homes, ranches, and environmental work around San Miguel County and nearby Ouray and Dolores counties.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost here
sections.html:
In this county you’re mostly drilling through fractured granite and gneiss, which is slower and tougher than plains alluvium. Typical drilling rates run about $65–$100 per foot. At the 182 ft median depth, that puts just the drilled hole around $11,800–$18,200.

By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished median-depth well pencils out around $17,800–$30,200. Because the middle half of wells spans 75–325 ft, you’ll want a bid that clearly spells out per‑foot rates past your allowance, and you should budget for the deeper end of that band in areas without good neighboring well logs.

sections.heading: Key risks: low yield, geology, and contamination
sections.html:
Geologically, the main risk here is fractured-bedrock variability. With 4% of tested wells under 1 gpm and 21% in the 1–5 gpm range, there’s a meaningful chance of a low producer on any given parcel. Those can often be managed with storage tanks and smart plumbing, but they’re a design and cost consideration.

On the environmental side, there are 12 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, about 1,093 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles in the county. That doesn’t mean your specific well is unsafe, but it does mean water-quality testing for metals and emerging contaminants is not optional. You’ll also need to lay out septic, well, and building envelopes so they meet current setback rules and avoid old mine workings.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in San Miguel County
sections.html:
Before closing on a parcel near Telluride, Norwood, Placerville, Sawpit, Ophir, or Mountain Village, pull the nearby well permits and look at actual depths, yields, and static levels. That will tell you if you’re in a pocket of 75–150 ft, or closer to the 300+ ft end of the county range.

On raw land, assume a household-use exempt well unless you have or can secure different water rights. Plan your budget using the 182 ft median cost figures, but be financially ready for a 300+ ft hole. Make your offer contingent on drilling success or at least on a credible drilling and septic layout review, including a full water test if there’s an existing well and awareness of nearby PFAS, mine, or cleanup sites.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in San Miguel County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on 2,016 wells that report total depth, the county-wide median is about 182 ft. Half of the wells fall between 75 and 325 ft. Around 31% are shallower than 100 ft, 38% sit between 100–300 ft, 25% run 300–600 ft, and about 7% go deeper than 600 ft, with an extreme case at 4,080 ft.

faq.q: How much water do wells in San Miguel County usually produce?
faq.a: Of the 717 wells with reported pump tests, the median yield is 7.0 gpm. The middle half range from 4.0 to 12.0 gpm. About 4% of wells make under 1 gpm, 21% produce 1–5 gpm, 54% are in the 5–15 gpm band, and 20% exceed 15 gpm. Most domestic wells have adequate production, but low-yield holes do occur.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in San Miguel County, CO?
faq.a: In the fractured granite and gneiss common here, typical drilling runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the 182 ft median depth, the borehole alone is roughly $11,800–$18,200. A complete system with casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical usually totals around $17,800–$30,200, depending on depth and site complexity.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in San Miguel County?
faq.a: The limited static water data (201 wells) don’t show a simple long-term decline. Median depth to water was about 125 ft in the 1990s, 185 ft in the 2000s, then shallowed to 60 ft in the 2010s and about 84 ft in the 2020s. That pattern likely reflects where wells were drilled each decade as much as any real regional trend. Always check recent nearby logs.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in San Miguel County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has 12 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, about 1,093 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within roughly 10 miles. Those regional factors mean you should plan on a full water test for any existing or new well, checking for metals, PFAS, and basic potability before relying on it.
